report:
The evidence actually contradicts the premise: rigorous long-term trials suggest saw palmetto does **not** outperform placebo for BPH symptoms.

**Key findings:**

- **CAMUS trial** (NEJM/JAMA Internal Medicine offshoot, published as "Effect of increasing doses of saw palmetto extract on lower urinary tract symptoms"), a large randomized, placebo-controlled trial testing standard and up to triple doses over 18 months, found no significant improvement in AUA Symptom Index scores compared with placebo, even at higher doses (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3979451/).

- **Cochrane systematic review** (Tacklind et al., 2012, updated 2023), pooling 32 RCTs and 5,666 men, is the most authoritative synthesis. In a meta-analysis of the two highest-quality long-term trials (n=582), Serenoa repens was not superior to placebo in reducing symptoms (mean difference 0.25 points on the AUA scale, 95% CI −0.58 to 1.07) — a null result. The review concludes saw palmetto alone provides "little to no benefit" (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD001423.pub3/abstract; https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001423_serenoa-repens-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia).

- Earlier, smaller, often industry-funded or shorter trials had shown modest symptom improvements, which fueled saw palmetto's popularity, but these were largely superseded by larger, more rigorous, longer-duration trials showing no effect (https://urologyandmenshealth.com/saw-palmetto-bph-evidence-review/).

**Conclusion:** The best current evidence—large, long-term, placebo-controlled trials and the definitive Cochrane meta-analysis—indicates saw palmetto does **not** meaningfully improve BPH symptoms compared to placebo in the longer term. Earlier positive findings likely reflected smaller sample sizes, shorter duration, publication bias, or extract variability. The premise that "yes" is correct appears **not supported** by the strongest available evidence.
